That's a great verse. You used the NLT, though, which sounded odd when I read it. So I compared it to a couple more precise translations.

Out of the anguish1 of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge2 shall3 the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. (ESV)

As a result of the anguish1 of His soul, He will see it and be satisfied; By His knowledge2 the Righteous One, My Servant, will3 justify the many, As He will bear their iniquities. (NASB)

When he sees all that is accomplished by his anguish1, he will be satisfied. And because of his experience2, my righteous servant will make it possible3 for many to be counted righteous, for he will bear all their sins. (NLT)

  1. At the first point of comparison, we see where the more precise translations give a literal rendering and the NLT gives the most common interpretation of seeing out of the anguish of his soul.

  2. At this point of comparison, the NLT picks one of several possible interpretations. Many interpreters take "by his knowledge" as being "by knowledge of him". That is, Isaiah here would be declaring that salvation will be through faith, true knowledge of Christ. Instead, NLT conspicuously exchanges "knowledge" for "experience". This seems like a less natural interpretation to me.

  3. The last point of comparison flat out changes major doctrine. The two more literal translations show the text saying Jesus "shall [...] make many to be accounted righteous", Jesus "will justify the many", in a definite sense. The NLT says that Jesus will merely "make it possible for many to be counted righteous". It changes the promise of God from doing to making it possible to do.

The NLT is far from the worst thing to use, but I don't think it's precise enough to study from.
